prize_parts.citation: For discoveries of the incretin hormone GLP-1, its physiological actions and active peptide form, which enabled a new class of therapies for type 2 diabetes and obesity

statement.case_for: All six openings placed B035 first, but agreement is not the argument. The case is the unbroken chain from hormone physiology to patient benefit: Holst's characterisation of GLP-1 secretion and the incretin effect, Mojsov's identification of the biologically active GLP-1(7-36) form, and Drucker's work on proglucagon-derived peptide biology and receptor action together explain why receptor agonism lowers glucose, suppresses appetite and, in large outcome trials, reduces cardiovascular and renal events. The mechanism has been confirmed by many independent groups and trials for over a decade, so the work is mature and the effect on medicine is large and well documented. As a neuroscientist I also note that the central satiety actions of GLP-1 add a neural-circuit dimension that makes the discovery physiologically richer than a pure endocrine story.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is attribution. Within three names the prize must separate peptide identification, physiology and drug development, and Knudsen's role in liraglutide and semaglutide is left out, as are early proglucagon contributors such as Habener who are not in the credited list. Mojsov's priority claim on the active peptide is disputed in the literature, and I cannot resolve it from the supplied record. If the committee reads the work as drug development rather than discovery, a physiology-centred citation may look too generous or too narrow depending on the reader. Long-term safety and durability of obesity treatment are still accruing, although I do not think this undermines the core discovery.

responses.point: Perlmann treats B035 as clearly first, but flags that credit among peptide identification, physiology and drug design is disputed and that it is unclear whether the committee prefers a physiology-centred or therapeutic-centred framing. He leaves out Knudsen.
responses.response: I agree with the exclusion of Knudsen under the three-person limit, but I would resist letting the framing question remain open. A citation anchored in physiology and the active peptide, rather than in a product, is the more defensible reading of the discovery criterion and also handles the industry-versus-academia problem. I share his concern that Mojsov's role is contested. I would still include her because the identification of the active truncated form is a decisive step that physiology alone does not supply, but I accept that this is the weakest link in the trio and would want the attribution evidence rechecked.

responses.point: Linnarsson ranks optogenetics (B046) second as a general method for causal cell-type-specific control, but notes that a prize for a tool rather than a disease mechanism may be weighed differently, and that six credited names exceed three slots.
responses.response: This is a fair qualification and I made the same ranking, so I will not defend B046 by field affinity. Its impact on circuit analysis, including the spinal and brainstem work I know, is real and well confirmed. But the attribution problem is more severe than for B035: any trio omits Bamberg, Boyden or Miesenböck, and my own Nagel, Hegemann and Deisseroth set is a judgement call that Linnarsson's own trio also makes. Given that, and the tool-versus-medicine question, I keep B046 as an alternative rather than the lead.

responses.point: Sandberg backs B035 with Drucker, Holst and Mojsov, but says the relative weight of Mojsov's role is contested; he also ranks cGAS-STING and CAR-T behind it and notes that the therapeutic payoff of STING remains unproven.
responses.response: I agree with Sandberg on the trio and on his caution about cGAS-STING: a mechanistically strong discovery without an approved therapy is early compared with GLP-1 and CAR-T. Where I differ slightly is on how much weight Mojsov's dispute should carry. A disputed priority claim is a reason to check the documentary record, not to drop her automatically, since dropping her would leave the identification of the active peptide uncredited.

responses.point: Wahren-Herlenius supports B035 but argues that Knudsen's role is largely industrial drug development, and ranks CAR-T second, noting uncertainty over early CAR concepts such as Eshhar's that are outside the credited list.
responses.response: I agree that Knudsen's contribution is real but sits on the development side, and that treating it as secondary is consistent with how the three-person limit forces a choice. On CAR-T I share her view that it is the strongest alternative, but I think the missing original CAR concept makes it a harder configuration than B035: June and Sadelain are the clearest pair, while Rosenberg's inclusion is arguable. That is why I keep B029 as an alternative and not as a second prize part, which would also push the union above three people.

uncertainties: Whether Mojsov's priority on the active GLP-1 peptide is adequately documented compared with other early proglucagon contributors outside the credited list.
Whether the committee would prefer to include Knudsen and drop one academic discoverer, which would change the framing from physiology to drug development.
How optogenetics (B046) should be weighed against a clinical discovery given six credited names and a three-person limit.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for B035, B029 or B046. My documented connections (a 2019 synthesis with Sten Grillner, collaborations with Patrik Ernfors, and a 2009 paper with Thomas Perlmann) concern motor-circuit and stem-cell work and do not involve any shortlisted candidate. Optogenetics is a method used in my field, but I have no documented tie to its credited individuals.
